note: Separates the duties of each supply chain actor and explains when a deployer inherits full provider obligations.
title: Obligations of importers, distributors and deployers of high-risk AI systems under the AI Act
explain_beginner: The EU AI Act does not just put obligations on the company that originally builds a high risk AI system, it also puts separate obligations on whoever imports it into Europe, whoever distributes or resells it, and whoever actually uses it day to day. This paper sorts out what each of those parties specifically has to do. Importers carry the heaviest burden among the three, essentially double checking that the original maker actually did what the law requires before the product enters the EU market. Distributors have lighter, narrower checks. The people or companies actually using the system, called deployers, have their own separate duties focused on how the system is used in practice, not on how it was built. The paper's most useful and slightly surprising point is that if someone in that chain modifies the AI system, even without meaning to change its purpose, they can suddenly be treated as if they were the original manufacturer, with all of that heavier set of legal duties.
explain_business: Any company anywhere in a high risk AI system's supply chain in Europe, importer, reseller, or the organization actually running the system, needs to know which of these three roles it occupies, because the compliance burden differs sharply between them, and misjudging the role risks real financial penalties under the Act. The single most actionable finding for procurement and engineering teams is that modifying a purchased AI system, retraining it, fine tuning it, or repurposing it for a new use case, can convert a deployer or distributor into something legally equivalent to the original provider overnight, carrying full conformity assessment and documentation duties that a company may not be prepared for. This applies now to any organization customizing off the shelf or vendor supplied high risk AI systems for EU markets, and the practical step it implies is auditing planned modifications against this reclassification risk before making them, not after.
explain_practitioner: This doctrinal legal analysis separates the AI Act's obligations across the high risk AI supply chain, finding that importers bear primary verification duties confirming a provider's compliance, such as checking conformity documentation exists, while distributors carry comparatively narrower diligence obligations. Deployers hold independent obligations that are not subordinate to the provider's, centered on managing risk during actual operational use rather than on design compliance. The paper's central finding is a reclassification scenario, when any actor in this chain modifies a high risk system or its intended purpose, that actor can inherit the full set of provider level obligations, including conformity assessment and technical documentation duties, because the Act treats AI systems as inherently susceptible to purpose drift regardless of original design intent. As a legal analysis rather than an empirical study, the paper offers no dataset, and its stated limitation is that properly identifying which role an actor occupies, particularly around what counts as a triggering modification, is a genuinely difficult interpretive problem in practice, not a settled bright line.
